title: How a messy circle becomes perfect
oneLine: The stroke is evened out, its corners are found with a recursive divide-and-conquer algorithm (RDP), a few shapes are fitted, and the one with the smallest error wins.

nodes.label: Trim the overlap
nodes.sub: cut what runs past the start

nodes.label: RDP in one line
nodes.sub: farthest point from the chord: if it is far, split there and recurse on both halves

steps.say: A mouse stroke is a list of points — many where you moved slowly, few where you were fast.
Resample: walk along the stroke and place 64 points at equal distances. Now every part counts the same. One pass: O(n).
Do the two ends meet? Compare the gap between first and last point with the size of the drawing.
If not, it is open: when the straight distance end-to-end is more than 93% of the stroke's length, it is a line (and snaps level or upright when close).
If it is a loop, the end usually runs a little past the start. That overlap would look like an extra corner, so it is cut off first.

Corners with RDP (Ramer–Douglas–Peucker), a divide-and-conquer recursion: find the point farthest from the line between the ends; if it is far, it is a corner — split there and do the same on both halves.
At the same time, fit an ellipse along the stroke's two main directions (PCA) and measure how far the points miss it.
Three corners make a triangle candidate; four right-angled corners a box. Each side sits at the middle (median) of its points, so one wobble cannot push it out.
The shape with the smallest error wins; an ellipse with nearly equal radii becomes a circle. All of this takes well under a millisecond.
